newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia retail sector seen flat in June qtr.
newsitem.headline: Australia retail sector seen flat in June qtr.

text.p: Australia's retail industry is likely to have improved slightly in June, but that will only leave the sector flat over the June quarter and do little to dent the case for a fifth rate cut, analysts said.

Thursday's data is expected to show that the volatile series -- it fell 1.7 percent in April only to rise 2.9 percent in May -- has posted a slight rise in June, just enough to see quarterly real trade scrape into positive territory.
The median forecast of the 25 economists Reuters surveyed was for a 0.4 percent rise in June retail trade. Forecasts ranged from a 1.5 percent fall to a 1.5 percent rise.
After a strong start to the year, sales weakened in March and April, raising market expectations of a rate cut.
Further weakness would see the odds shorten on another rate cut, and so the June data is expected to be the most closely watched figure of the week.
"We really don't expect a number which will dissuade the Reserve Bank from moving in the next week or two to cut rates again," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
While a rise is the median forecast, it is not expected across the board, with some expecting a correction to May's strength, and also pointing to changing shopping habits.
"We see retail trade in the month dropping 0.2 percent. As consumers wait for the July sales they will tend to delay their purchases," said Merrill Lynch chief economist Nigel Douglas.

The June data would also contain the retail trade for the June quarter in constant price terms, one of the first pieces of information the economists would receive on second quarter gross domestic product.
Economists expect that after the weak April figure, the strong rise in May and the slight rise in June would be enough to keep real retail trade in positive territory.
Forecasts for the quarterly figure centre on a 0.1 percent rise, and range from a 0.5 percent fall to a 0.8 percent rise.

In the March quarter, real retail trade rose 2.2 percent, so while consumption is not expected to make a large contribution to second quarter GDP, economists said a rise would suggest a reasonable performance over the first half of 1997.

Real retail trade extracts the effect of prices from sales volume, and the range of forecasts reflect not only differing opinions on how sales fared in June, but also expectations of the retail deflator.

The retail trade deflator -- which adjusts for price changes -- is expected to reflect the pressure that retailers are feeling on their ability, or more currently their lack of it, to pass on price increases to consumers.
This has helped keep inflation low, and a low deflator would bias the quarterly sales figure to the upside, economists said
"For a year and a half now, retail prices have risen by less than the underlying inflation rate, but that gap widened in fact in the last two quarters," Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields.
Data last week showed underlying inflation rose 0.3 percent in the June quarter.
"So we could see a bit of that Thursday with the retail deflator, which would have the effect, if it came through, of boosting the real figure just a little bit," he said.
Economists said that while the retail data may have little influence on the RBA's thinking on whether or not to cut rates, it would have an impact on market expectations.

"I think it is logical the Bank would wait to see this data, but I don't think it's likely to change its mind about a rate cut given the inflation and particaularly the wages data we saw last week," Shields said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
